title: The Time to Live Model: An Integrated Self-Regulation Framework for Sustainable Behavior Change
content: Behavior change is frequently initiated but less reliably maintained. Individuals may establish meaningful intentions and begin acting toward desired outcomes, yet discontinue new patterns when initial motivation decreases, competing goals emerge, resources become constrained, or personal and environmental conditions change. Existing theories provide well-developed explanations for particular components of this process, including goal selection, motivational quality, attentional control, self-monitoring, habit formation, environmental opportunity, and social support. However, these mechanisms are often examined within separate theoretical traditions. This conceptual article introduces the Time to Live (TTL) Model, an integrated self-regulation framework for understanding sustainable behavior change through five interdependent regulatory conditions: clarity, energy, focus, awareness, and support. Clarity concerns meaningful direction and alignment between behavior, goals, and personally relevant values. Energy refers to the psychological and physical capacity available for continued goal-directed action. Focus concerns the allocation and protection of attention in the presence of competing demands. Awareness enables monitoring of behavior, progress, internal states, and changing circumstances, allowing adaptive correction. Support encompasses interpersonal, environmental, and structural resources that facilitate continued action. The TTL Model proposes that sustainable behavior change depends not solely on initial motivation, intention strength, or willpower, but on the coordinated functioning of these five conditions over time. Its distinctive theoretical contribution is configurational: a substantial deficit in one component may become a regulatory bottleneck, destabilizing behavior maintenance even when other components remain relatively strong. The model further conceptualizes lapses not as definitive failures but as regulatory information that can activate monitoring, adaptation, and behavioral recovery. Drawing on research in self-regulation, goal-setting, self-concordance, subjective vitality, attentional control, implementation intentions, progress monitoring, habit formation, psychological flexibility, goal adjustment, and social support, the article develops testable propositions and outlines a program for empirical validation.
